{{Short description|US cryobiologist and businessman}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=June 2022}}

'''Gregory Michael Fahy'''<ref>{{cite web | title = Method of introduction and removal of high concentrations of cryoprotectants by vascular perfusion | publisher = [[Justia]] |url=https://patents.justia.com/patent/11659835 | access-date =2024-07-30 }}</ref> is a California-based [[cryobiology|cryobiologist]], [[Biogerontology|biogerontologist]], and businessman. He is the vice president and chief scientific officer at [[21st Century Medicine]], Inc, and has co-founded Intervene Immune, a company developing clinical methods to reverse immune system aging.<ref name="nature-triim">{{cite journal |last1=Abbott |first1=Alison |title=First hint that body's 'biological age' can be reversed |journal=Nature |page=173 |language=en |doi=10.1038/d41586-019-02638-w |date=September 5, 2019|volume=573 |issue=7773 |pmid=31506619 |bibcode=2019Natur.573..173A |s2cid=202159998 |doi-access= }}</ref> He was the 2022–2023 president of the [[Society for Cryobiology]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Leadership | work = Executive Director and Officers 2020–2021 | publisher = [[Society for Cryobiology]] |url= https://www.societyforcryobiology.org/leadership | access-date =2022-01-19 }}</ref>

== Education ==
A native of California, Fahy holds a Bachelor of Science degree in [[biology]] from the [[University of California, Irvine]] and a PhD in [[pharmacology]] and [[cryobiology]] from the [[Medical College of Georgia|Medical College of Georgia in Augusta]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Gregory M. Fahy, Ph.D. | work = Business Management Team | publisher = [[21st Century Medicine]]  | date = 1999–2008 | url = https://www.21cm.com/management.html  | access-date =2022-01-19 }}</ref>

He currently serves on the board of directors of two organizations{{which|date=October 2023}} and as a referee for numerous scientific journals and funding agencies, and holds 35 patents on cryopreservation methods, aging interventions, transplantation, and other topics.{{cn|date=June 2023}}

==Career==

Fahy is the world's foremost expert in organ cryopreservation by [[Cryopreservation#Vitrification|vitrification]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Fahy GM, Wowk B, Wu J, Phan J, Rasch C, Chang A, Zendejas E | title=Cryopreservation of organs by vitrification: perspectives and recent advances | journal=Cryobiology  | volume=48 | issue=2 | year=2004 | pages=157–178 | url = http://www.21cm.com/pdfs/cryopreservation_advances.pdf | pmid=15094092 | doi=10.1016/j.cryobiol.2004.02.002}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Fahy GM, Wowk B, Wu J | title=Cryopreservation of complex systems: the missing link in the regenerative medicine supply chain | journal=[[Rejuvenation Research]] | volume=9 | issue=2 | year=2006 | pages=279–291 | url = http://www.21cm.com/articles/Missing_Link.pdf | pmid=16706656 | doi=10.1089/rej.2006.9.279}}</ref><ref name="KidVit">{{cite journal |vauthors=Fahy GM, Wowk B, Pagotan R, Chang A, Phan J, Thomson B, Phan L | title=Physical and biological aspects of renal vitrification| journal=Organogenesis  | volume=5 | issue=3 | year=2009 | pages=167–175  | pmid=20046680 | pmc=2781097 | doi=10.4161/org.5.3.9974}}</ref> Fahy introduced the modern successful approach to vitrification for [[cryopreservation]] in cryobiology<ref>{{cite book |author1=Michael J. Taylor |author2=Ying C. Song |author3=Kelvin G.M. Brockbank |  title = Vitrification in Tissue Preservation: New Developments In: ''Life in the Frozen State'' (B.J. Fuller, N. Lane, and E.E. Benson, Eds.)  | publisher = [[CRC Press]] | pages =  603–641 | year = 2004 | isbn = 978-0-415-24700-9 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Fahy, G.M.  |author2=Hirsh, A. |  title =  Prospects for Organ Preservation by Vitrification. In: ''Organ Preservation, Basic and Applied Aspects'' (D.E. Pegg, I.A. Jacobsen and N.A. Halasz, Eds.)  | publisher = [[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] | pages =  399–404 | year = 1982 | isbn = 978-0-85200-418-0 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Fahy GM, MacFarlane DR, Angell CA, Meryman HT | title=Vitrification as an approach to cryopreservation | journal=Cryobiology  | volume=21 | issue=4 | year=1984 | pages=407–426 | pmid=6467964 | doi=10.1016/0011-2240(84)90079-8}}</ref><ref name="Nature">{{cite journal |vauthors=Rall WF, Fahy GM | title=Ice-free cryopreservation of mouse embryos at -196 degrees C by vitrification | journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]  | volume=313 | issue=6003 | year=1985 | pages=573–575 | pmid=3969158 | doi=10.1038/313573a0| s2cid=4351126 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author=Fahy GM | title=Vitrification: a new approach to organ cryopreservation| journal=Progress in Clinical and Biological Research  | volume=224 | year=1986 | pages=305–335 | pmid=3540994}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last = Fahy | first = Gregory M. | title = Vitrification versus Freezing of Organs | work = [[Science (journal)|Science]] E-Letter responses | publisher = [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]   | date = May 16, 2002 | url = http://www.sciencemag.org/cgi/eletters/296/5568/655d | access-date = October 22, 2010 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Fahy, G.M. |author2=Rall, W.F.  |  title = Vitrification: An overview. In: ''Vitrification in Assisted Reproduction: A User's Manual and Troubleshooting Guide'' (J. Liebermann and M.J. Tucker, Eds)  | publisher = Informa Healthcare | year = 2007 | isbn = 978-0-415-40882-0 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Mullen, S.F. |author2=Fahy, G.M.  |  title =  Fundamental aspects of vitrification as a method of reproductive cell, tissue, and organ cryopreservation. In: ''Principles & Practice of Fertility Preservation'' (Donnez, J., and Kim, S.S., Eds.)  | publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]] | date = February 28, 2011 | isbn = 978-0-521-19695-6 }}</ref> and he is widely credited, along with William F.&nbsp;Rall, for introducing vitrification into the field of [[reproductive biology]].<ref name="Nature" /><ref>{{cite journal | title=Cryopreservation of embryos | journal=[[The Lancet]] | volume=1 | issue=8430 | year=1985 | page=678 | pmid=2858625 | doi=10.1016/s0140-6736(85)91336-4| s2cid=45190786 }}</ref>

In 2005, where he was a keynote speaker at the annual Society for Cryobiology meeting, Fahy announced that 21st Century Medicine had successfully cryopreserved a rabbit kidney at −130&nbsp;°C by vitrification and transplanted it into a rabbit after rewarming, with subsequent long-term life support by the vitrified-rewarmed kidney as the sole kidney. This research breakthrough was later published in the peer-reviewed journal ''Organogenesis''.<ref name="KidVit" />

Fahy is also a [[Biogerontology|biogerontologist]] and is the originator and editor-in-chief of ''The Future of Aging: Pathways to Human Life Extension'', a multi-authored book on the future of [[biogerontology]].<ref>{{cite book |editor1=Gregory M. Fahy |editor2=Michael D. West |editor3=L. Stephen Coles |editor4=Steven B. Harris | title = The Future of Aging: Pathways to Human Life Extension  | publisher = [[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] | date = October 2010 | isbn = 978-90-481-3998-9 }}</ref> He currently serves on the editorial boards of ''[[Rejuvenation Research]]'' and the ''Open Geriatric Medicine Journal'' and served for 16 years as a director of the [[American Aging Association]] and for 6 years as the editor of ''AGE News'', the organization's newsletter.

== Research ==

As a scientist with the [[American Red Cross]], Fahy was the originator of the first practical method of cryopreservation by vitrification and the inventor of computer-based systems to apply this technology to whole [[organ (anatomy)|organs]]. Before joining Twenty-First Century Medicine, he was the chief scientist for Organ, Inc and of LRT, Inc. He was also Head of the Tissue Cryopreservation Section of the [[Blood transfusion|Transfusion]] and Cryopreservation Research Program of the [[National Naval Medical Center|U.S. Naval Medical Research Institute]] in [[Bethesda, Maryland]] where he spearheaded the original concept of ice blocking agents. In 2014, he was named a Fellow of the Society for Cryobiology in recognition of the impact of his work in low temperature biology.<ref>{{cite web |title=Science & Business Management Teams |url=https://www.21cm.com/management.html |publisher=[[21st Century Medicine]] |access-date=August 1, 2020}}</ref>

In 2015–2017, Fahy led the TRIIM (Thymus Regeneration, Immunorestoration, and Insulin Mitigation) human clinical trial, designed to reverse aspects of human aging. The purpose of the TRIIM trial was to investigate the possibility of using recombinant human [[growth hormone]] (rhGH) to prevent or reverse signs of immunosenescence in ten 51‐ to 65‐year‐old putatively healthy men. The study:
<blockquote>
Observed protective immunological changes, improved risk indices for many age‐related diseases, and a mean epigenetic age approximately 1.5 years less than baseline after 1 year of treatment (−2.5‐year change compared to no treatment at the end of the study).<ref name="nature-triim" />
</blockquote>

== Awards==

Fahy was named as a [[Fellow]] of the [[Society for Cryobiology]] in 2014,<ref>{{cite web |title=Newsnotes June 2014 |url=https://www.societyforcryobiology.org/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=94:sfc_newsletter_june_2014&catid=19:site-content |publisher=[[Society for Cryobiology]]}}</ref> and in 2010 he received the Distinguished Scientist Award for Reproductive Biology from the Reproductive Biology Professional Group of the American Society of Reproductive Medicine.{{cn|date=March 2022}}  He received the Cryopreservation Award from the International Longevity and Cryopreservation Summit held in Madrid, Spain in 2017 in recognition of his career in and dedication to the field of [[cryobiology]]. Fahy also received the Grand Prize for Medicine from INPEX in 1995 for his invention of computerized organ cryoprotectant perfusion technology. In 2005, he was recognized as a Fellow of the [[American Aging Association]].{{cn|date=March 2022}}
